prohibited_recommendations: Do not prescribe anticholinergic medications (oxybutynin for the urinary urgency, first-generation antihistamines, tricyclics), which worsen cognition in this population
Do not start an antipsychotic for the apathy — it is not psychosis, and antipsychotics carry an excess mortality warning in dementia
Do not add a second antiplatelet agent or an anticoagulant: there is no cardioembolic indication and the deep microbleeds raise the haemorrhagic risk
Do not attribute the decline to normal ageing or to depression without completing the workup
Do not lower blood pressure abruptly in a patient with severe small-vessel disease; titrate to target rather than dropping precipitously
required_recommendations: Recognise the two transient episodes of right-hand clumsiness and dysarthria as probable lacunar events, each followed by a step down, and continue single antiplatelet therapy (aspirin 100 mg daily) for secondary prevention [AHA_ASA_2021_secondary]

Lower blood pressure (168/92 mmHg, irregular amlodipine) gradually to below 130/80 mmHg, addressing adherence first and checking orthostatic BP at each change given the two falls [AHA_ASA_2021_secondary]
Intensify lipid lowering (LDL 118 mg/dL on atorvastatin 40 mg): check adherence and increase to atorvastatin 80 mg [AHA_ASA_2021_secondary]
Individualise the HbA1c target to about below 8.0% (current 8.4%) and avoid hypoglycaemia [ADA_older_adults_2026]
Address driving with a formal driving assessment, since he still drives
Address falls (physiotherapy and a home review after two falls on turning), urinary urgency without anticholinergic drugs, alcohol reduction and support for his wife

avoided_actions.rationale: Stepwise decline over three years without fluctuation, seizures or rapid progression; EEG would not change the diagnosis.

No rest tremor, cogwheel rigidity, fluctuations, hallucinations or dream enactment; the hypomimia and short steps come with preserved arm swing and pyramidal signs, so a dopamine transporter scan is not indicated.
No Lewy body features; cardiac sympathetic imaging does not address his syndrome.
A three-year stepwise decline with vascular risk factors is not the subacute multidomain syndrome for which paraneoplastic or autoimmune encephalitis antibodies are indicated.
MRI is available and not contraindicated; CT cannot show microbleeds, siderosis or small lacunes.
Lacunar events explained by small-vessel disease, without cortical or multi-territory infarcts; prolonged rhythm monitoring would not change management.

accepted: Vascular dementia: subcortical ischaemic (small-vessel) type, sporadic hypertensive arteriopathy
major neurocognitive disorder due to vascular disease

differential.key_features: The profile is executive and psychomotor with cue-responsive recall, the medial temporal lobes are preserved at Scheltens 1, and the course is stepwise rather than insidiously progressive
No hippocampal atrophy and no clinical or imaging feature suggesting a second degenerative process; biomarkers were not required to reach the threshold for attribution here
Gait is short-stepped rather than magnetic, the Evans index is 0.28 with ventriculomegaly proportionate to atrophy, and there is no disproportionately enlarged subarachnoid space
No fluctuating cognition, no visual hallucinations, no spontaneous parkinsonism and no dream enactment
Geriatric Depression Scale 5/15, and the imaging burden with focal neurological signs is not explained by mood

key_clinical_evidence: Vascular attribution here rests on the lesion pattern, not only on the history: Fazekas 3 confluent white matter hyperintensity with five lacunes is by itself sufficient under VASCOG 2014 to attribute a dementia to small-vessel disease

The cognitive profile is the discriminator: executive and processing-speed impairment with recall that improves on cueing is a retrieval pattern; Alzheimer's disease produces a storage pattern in which cueing does not help
Gait is part of the syndrome, not a separate problem — the short-stepped wide-based gait with preserved arm swing localises to the same subcortical networks as the cognitive deficit

Two deep microbleeds in a thalamic and pontine distribution indicate hypertensive arteriopathy; strictly lobar microbleeds would have meant amyloid angiopathy and would have changed the antithrombotic decision
Poor adherence to antihypertensive therapy is the single most modifiable driver of progression and is more valuable to establish than any further imaging

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Diabetic distal sensory loss is real and contributes to unsteadiness, but it does not explain the cognitive syndrome or the wide-based low-clearance gait with brisk knee reflexes and extensor plantar response
red_herrings.intended_effect: Suggests a peripheral neuropathy as an alternative explanation for the gait disorder

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: The Evans index is 0.28 with ventricular enlargement proportionate to parenchymal loss and no disproportionately enlarged subarachnoid space — this is ex vacuo dilatation, not hydrocephalus
red_herrings.intended_effect: Prompts a diagnosis of normal pressure hydrocephalus and an unnecessary tap test

sequence_constraints.reason: Document the cognitive deficit before attributing it: imaging read without a cognitive profile invites over-attribution of incidental white matter change

metadata.difficulty_rationale: Unambiguous severe small-vessel burden with a matching executive-predominant profile and a stepwise history; the only distractors are diabetic sensory loss and ex vacuo ventriculomegaly
key_educational_points: A dementia can be attributed to small-vessel disease on the lesion pattern when the burden is severe, even when the clinical events that marked its steps were never investigated
Cue-responsive delayed recall separates the retrieval deficit of subcortical disease from the storage deficit of Alzheimer's disease
Microbleed distribution carries therapeutic weight: deep means hypertensive, strictly lobar means amyloid angiopathy
Objective gait testing belongs in the dementia assessment when a subcortical mechanism is suspected

patient.history_present_illness: Mr. Aldo Ferretti is a 74-year-old retired railway signalling technician brought by his wife for evaluation of three years of cognitive and gait decline. She dates the beginning precisely: three years ago he had an episode of right hand clumsiness and slurred speech at breakfast that resolved within the hour and for which he never sought care. In the weeks after it he became noticeably slower — slower to answer, slower to dress, slower to follow a conversation with more than two people in it. He plateaued for over a year, and then a second similar episode two years ago was followed by another step down: since then he has stopped doing the household accounts, which he had kept meticulously for four decades, and has twice paid the same electricity bill twice. His wife emphasises that his memory for events is comparatively good — he recalls conversations, visitors and appointments if he is given a hint about the context — but that he cannot organise or plan, loses the thread when interrupted, and has become apathetic, sitting in front of the television for hours without complaint. Walking changed in parallel: small steps, feet barely leaving the ground, and two falls in the past six months, both while turning in the kitchen. He has urinary urgency and has had two episodes of incontinence. There are no visual hallucinations, no fluctuations in alertness across the day, no dream enactment, and no resting tremor. His blood pressure has been repeatedly above target at the general practice, and he acknowledges taking his amlodipine irregularly.

neurological_exam.additional: No resting tremor, no cogwheel rigidity at the wrists. Frontal release signs present (palmomental, glabellar tap unsuppressed). No myoclonus. Urinary urgency for the past year with two episodes of incontinence.
neurological_exam.coordination: Finger-to-nose accurate. Heel-to-shin mildly clumsy bilaterally without dysmetria on target.
neurological_exam.cranial_nerves: Pupils equal and reactive. Extraocular movements full, saccades mildly hypometric. Visual fields full. Mild bilateral facial hypomimia. Palate elevates symmetrically. Tongue midline.
neurological_exam.gait: Short-stepped and wide-based with reduced foot clearance and preserved arm swing. Turns taken in five small steps. Tandem gait impossible after two steps. Romberg negative. No festination, no freezing.
neurological_exam.mental_status: Alert and cooperative; oriented to person, place and year, date incorrect. Slow to initiate answers, with long response latencies his wife fills in; conversation coherent. Naming and repetition intact in conversation. No apraxia, no neglect. Formal cognitive screening reported separately.
neurological_exam.motor: Normal bulk. Tone increased in both legs with a spastic catch at the knees. Strength 5/5 throughout apart from 4+/5 hip flexion bilaterally. No pronator drift, no tremor.
neurological_exam.reflexes: 3+ at both knees, 2+ at the ankles, plantar responses extensor on the right and equivocal on the left. Palmomental reflex present bilaterally.
neurological_exam.sensory: Vibration reduced at both ankles (6 seconds, 128 Hz tuning fork). Light touch, pinprick and proprioception otherwise intact.
